item.title: Baseline radiographic and microbiologic predictors of treatment outcomes in a shortened all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB
item.description:
Edmund Q. L. Shen, Stephane Mpinda, Llang Maama, Meseret Tamirat, Phate Sebakeng, Lawrence Oyewusi, Allison LaHood, Letizia Trevisi, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78700-9
Abstract WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. We conducted a prospective cohort study (NCT05871489) of adults with bacteriologically-confirmed pulmonary MDR/RR-TB treated with a shortened, all-oral regimen in Lesotho. We evaluated baseline microbiologic and radiographic features and their associations with time-to-culture-conversion, end-of-treatment outcomes, and final post-treatment outcomes. Among 238 participants (median age 41 [IQR:31–56], 29% female, 62% with HIV), there were 27 unfavorable outcomes (20 deaths, 3 treatment failures, 4 recurrences). 142 of 148 (95.9%) with positive baseline cultures experienced conversion within four months. Fibrosis, cavitation, bilateral disease, and high smear grade were associated with delayed culture conversion and lower odds of treatment success. Bilateral disease was more strongly associated with unfavorable outcomes in those without HIV; fibrosis and high smear grade showed stronger associations among those with HIV. Cavitation with high smear grade (uOR=0.29, 95%CI:0.11–0.78; aOR=0.39, 95%CI:0.14-1.14), and severe fibrocavitary disease (multi-lobar fibrosis and at least one cavity ≥5 cm) (uOR=0.20, 95%CI:0.07–0.64; aOR=0.26, 95%CI:0.07-0.94) were negatively associated with favorable final outcomes. These findings suggest that baseline sputum and chest radiographic features—particularly in-combination—identify higher-risk patients and may inform risk-adapted strategies for shortened all-oral MDR/RR-TB regimens.

item.title: Rationally micropatterned antifogging hydrogels counteracting extreme condensation
item.description:
Hyunchul Park, Cheuk Wing Edmond Lam, Iwan Haechler, Thomas M. Schutzius, Dimos Poulikakos
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78429-5
Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Conventional antifogging strategies relying on hydrophilic or hydrophobic coatings, based on chemistry and/or nano-topography, can counteract up to mild water deposition, but lose functionality at excessive condensation environments. Here, we present a passive approach, rationally micropatterning an inherently hydrophilic hydrogel to maintain high transparency under supersaturation. Guided by optics and wetting theory, and employing a diffusion model to calculate related timescales of water film formation, we engineer a wicking structure on poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel, facilitating long-term sustainable filmwise condensation. Employing quantitative optical clarity measurements and visualization, we show that our approach clearly outperforms state-of-the-art antifogging alternatives, retaining high optical clarity even in boiling environments. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.

item.title: Lesions of anterior cingulate cortex disrupt an electrophysiological signature of goal completion in humans
item.description:
Joyce Oerlemans, Ricardo J. Alejandro, Dimitri Hemelsoet, Eva Genbrugge, Katie Bouche, Luc Defreyne, Veerle De Herdt, Clay B. Holroyd
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78450-8
Abstract The reward positivity (RewP) is an event-related brain potential (ERP) component associated with feedback and goal completion. Although the component is said to be generated in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), this inference is disputed because of the inverse problem. Recent intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) current source density analyses provided direct evidence that the RewP is generated in caudal ACC, specifically Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’. To further test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of damage to frontal cortex damage on RewP amplitude. Scalp EEG was recorded from 68 stroke patients with frontal lesions while they performed a trial-and-error guessing task used to elicit a canonical RewP. Non-parametric voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping revealed that damage to Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’ significantly attenuated RewP amplitude. These results align with evidence suggesting a single generator of the RewP in the caudal ACC, supporting the role of caudal ACC in motivation of extended behaviors.

item.title: Low-Dose Glucocorticoids Adjunctive to Flow Diverter Therapy for Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms Improve Cerebrovascular Outcomes
item.description:
Zhuohua Wen, Xiheng Chen, Xin Tong, Chi Huang, Mengshi Huang, Jiancheng Lin, Anqi Xu, Hanyan Yang, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78408-w
Abstract Flow diverter (FD) implantation is standard for unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), but cerebrovascular complications persist. This nested study within a prospective multicenter cohort evaluates whether short-term, low-dose glucocorticoid use is associated with cerebrovascular outcomes after FD implantation. Propensity-score matching with exact matching on UIA location yielded 1327 patients (360 glucocorticoid-treated; 967 controls). Intravenous glucocorticoids, initiated within 2 hours of the FD procedure and administered for ≥2 days, were associated with fewer in-hospital cerebrovascular events (6.9% vs. 13.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53) and major cerebrovascular events (4.7% vs. 12.4%; aOR, 0.37). Over a median 2-year follow-up, glucocorticoid use was also associated with fewer new-onset major cerebrovascular events (3.6% vs. 8.7%; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.41) and less in-stent stenosis (7.9% vs. 13.2%; aOR, 0.55). Findings remained robust in unmatched patients on sensitivity analyses. We demonstrate that perioperative glucocorticoid regimens may reduce cerebrovascular events and in-stent stenosis in FD-treated patients, warranting randomized trials.

item.title: Accounting for longitudinal peak quality metrics with MSstats+ enhances differential analysis in proteomic experiments with data-independent acquisition
item.description:
Devon Kohler, Eralp Dogu, Mrittika Bhattacharya, Ozge Karayel, Manuel Magana, Anthony Wu, Veronica G. Anania, Olga Vitek
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78591-w
Abstract Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. Despite continued improvements, the quality of quantification may be poor for some measurements. As the scale of proteomic experiments increases, these poor-quality measurements are challenging to characterize by hand, yet they undermine the detection of differentially abundant proteins and the downstream biological conclusions. We introduce MSstats + , a computational workflow that takes as input not only peak intensities reported by tools such as Spectronaut or DIA-NN, but also quality metrics such as peak shape and retention time, and longitudinal run order profiles of these metrics. MSstats+ translates these metrics into a single measure of quality, and downweights poor quality measurements when detecting differentially abundant proteins. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. MSstats+ is implemented in the family of open-source R/Bioconductor packages MSstats.

item.title: A CRC–MYB chromatin loop controls auxin-mediated nectary growth in Arabidopsis
item.description:
Hideaki Iimura, Makoto Takahashi, Ryosuke Ohta, Asumi Nagamori, Seika Togawa, Yuki Furuta, Koki Nakamura, Febri Yuda Kurniawan, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78943-6
Abstract Floral nectaries, typically located at stamen bases, secrete sugar-rich nectar containing diverse secondary metabolites. Despite their defined position and specialized function, the mechanisms governing nectary formation remain unclear. Using publicly available single-nucleus RNA-seq data and newly generated spatial transcriptomic data, we identify a putative ordering of transcriptional states associated with nectary development and a spatial regulatory network controlling nectary growth in Arabidopsis thaliana . We further show that CRABS CLAW (CRC) is central to this network, integrating transcriptional regulation with spatial auxin transport and pathways controlling phytohormone signaling, sugar transport and terpene biosynthesis. CRC interacts with MYB21, MYB24 and MYB57 to form a complex that binds the 5′ and 3′ regulatory regions of MACCHI-BOU 4 ( MAB4 ), promoting a chromatin loop that enhances MAB4 expression and supports proper nectary size. MAB4 reinforces PIN-FORMED 1-mediated auxin transport to establish auxin maxima at the nectary tip and regulates PIN6 localization to maintain auxin gradients. These findings link transcriptional regulation and auxin transport with nectary organogenesis and metabolic function.

item.title: Multimodal substrate recruitment enables CTLHMKLN1 E3 ligase to target acetylated N-, C-, and internal degrons
item.description:
Sara Sepic, Karthik V. Gottemukkala, Jiale Du, Samuel A. Maiwald, Jakub Chrustowicz, Eleftheria C. Papadopoulou, Luca J. Stier, Susanne von Gronau, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78311-4
Abstract The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLH MKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. Here, we reconstitute CTLH MKLN1 -dependent ubiquitylation of three biochemically distinct substrates – MKLN1 itself, ZMYND19, and FAM72A-recruited UNG2, and determine cryo-EM structures of each substrate bound to MKLN1. The structures reveal how MKLN1’s discoidin and Kelch β-propeller domains engage substrates through multivalent contacts. MKLN1 recruits itself through discoidin-Kelch interactions between MKLN1 dimers, forming an assembly that competes with other substrates. ZMYND19 and FAM72A each bind to MKLN1 through loops engaging the discoidin trench domain while their C-terminal Arg residues engage the MKLN1 Kelch central channel, identifying MKLN1 as an Arg/C-degron receptor. The acetylated N-terminus of UNG2 is positioned within a Y-shaped tunnel of FAM72A, defining an adaptor-mediated Ac/N-degron recognition mechanism. Thus, our data reveal how combinatorial deployment of MKLN1 discoidin and Kelch domains enable a single receptor subunit to recognize a diverse substrate repertoire, adding to a complex picture of degron recognition across the GID/CTLH family.

item.title: Developing and benchmarking one health genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus in wastewater
item.description:
Minxi Jiang, Audrey L. W. Wang, James B. Thissen, Kara L. Nelson, Lenore Pipes, Rose S. Kantor
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78683-7
Abstract Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a persistent One Health threat, and whole-genome sequencing from wastewater offers a promising surveillance tool. However, IAV is at low abundance in wastewater, making it difficult to sequence. We benchmark four targeted enrichment methods suited for multi-subtype whole-genome IAV sequencing including custom and off-the-shelf methods. Our custom HA tiled-amplicon panel is sensitive, fast, and cost-effective, making it suitable for monitoring low-abundance seasonal variants of known subtypes, although its reliance on conserved and intact primer-binding sites limits primer design to fewer subtypes. A published universal amplicon method targets all IAV subtypes but performs poorly in wastewater due to its reliance on intact genome segments. Meanwhile, probe-capture methods are resilient to RNA degradation. In real wastewater samples, our custom probe panel recovers whole-genome signals from circulating H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, including validated H5N1 2.3.4.4b reads in samples where dPCR detection is limited. However, probe-capture is generally more costly and labor-intensive than amplicon methods. Across all four sequencing methods, two wastewater matrices, and most spike-in and endogenous virus targets, ultrafiltration-based virus concentration consistently outperforms large-volume direct extraction. Together, these benchmarking comparisons and custom panels provide needed information for implementing IAV genomic sequencing in routine wastewater surveillance.

item.title: Confining chlorine in the cation solvation sheaths towards stable and sustainable seawater electrolysis
item.description:
Peng-Cheng Yu, Ye-Hua Wang, Xiao-Long Zhang, Shu-Ping Sun, Tao Fang, Xu-Ying-Nan Tao, Yu Yang, Jie Liao, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78207-3
Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. We report that in situ segregated fluorine can actuate the desolvation of cations and Cl − ions via strong H ∙ ∙ ∙ F bonding, leading to the formation of intimate cation-Cl − contact ion pairs that make Cl − migration toward electrode surface prohibited. Meanwhile, fluorine remaining in the cobalt-based catalyst shortens the Co–Co distance, attributable to its large electronegativity, triggering an oxide path mechanism that circumvents the nonideal scaling between OH * and OOH * during oxygen-evolving reaction. Direct seawater electrolysis (with 1 M NaOH) incorporating this catalyst achieves 1 ampere per square centimeter (A cm −2 ) at 1.7 volts and maintains at 0.5 A cm −2 and 60 °C over 2,450 hours degrading at 24.9 microvolts per hour. Our catalyst even survives repeatedly switched current densities (0.25, 0.5, and 1 A cm −2 ) for more than 1,250 hours, manifesting compatibility with fluctuating renewable electricity.

item.title: Coordinated control of both microtubule ends regulates mitotic spindle length
item.description:
Shane A. Fiorenza, Sheba Cheeran, Elena Doria, Iva M. Tolić, Patrick Meraldi, Nenad Pavin
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78426-8
Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Here we introduce a model which demonstrates that length-dependent regulation at both microtubule ends allows plus- and minus-end dynamics to synchronize with one another, enabling pathways of poleward-flux-based spindle length control which rectify previous results. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

item.title: Infant hippocampal and amygdala volume in an observational follow-up from a randomized clinical trial for maternal prenatal depression
item.description:
Catherine H. Demers, Benjamin L. Hankin, LillyBelle K. Deer, Robert J. Gallop, Mercedes Hoeflich Haase, M. Camille Hoffman, Martin A. Styner, Nancy K. Grote, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78276-4
Abstract Prenatal maternal depression may have intergenerational effects on offspring brain development, with potential socioemotional consequences. This observational follow-up study examines brain development and subsequent negative emotionality among 109 infants born to mothers participating in a randomized clinical trial (NCT03011801). In the prior trial, brief interpersonal psychotherapy significantly reduced prenatal depression symptoms and disorder as the published primary and secondary endpoints. Exploratory infant outcomes include hippocampal and amygdala volumes at 6 weeks and negative emotionality at 6 months. Here we show that infants of mothers randomized to interpersonal psychotherapy during pregnancy have lower right hippocampal volume than infants of mothers in the enhanced usual care group ( p = .002, d = 0.62). No statistically significant group differences are observed in left hippocampal or amygdala volume. Smaller hippocampal volume predicts subsequent lower negative emotionality (r = 0.19, p = 0.045). In this study, a maternal prenatal depression intervention is associated with differences in infant brain development with implications for their subsequent emotional health.

item.description:
Yuya Kinoshita, Michio Sato, Tsuyoshi Kadomatsu, Manami Katoh, Kazutaka Ikeda, Goro Yoshioka, Yuya Matsue, Wataru Fujimoto, et al.

DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78375-2
Abstract Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains a major unmet clinical challenge. Although obesity is common in many HFpEF cohorts from Europe and North America, three Japanese HFpEF cohorts identified hypertension and sympathetic overactivation, rather than obesity, as dominant features. item.title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
item.description:
Satya Prakash, Clenira Varela, Mark Walsh, Roberto Galizi, Mark Isalan, Alfonso Jaramillo
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78417-9
Abstract Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

item.description:
Daria Khuntsariya, Umut Batman, Arya Krishnan, Souradip Mukherjee, Daniel Rozbesky, Florent Lemaitre, Carsten Janke, Virginie Hamel, et al.

DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78500-1

item.description:

Abstract To protect themselves against phage infection, bacteria employ diverse defense systems that are typically activated specifically upon infection. item.title: MxB N-terminus adopts a stable α-helix to engage the HIV-1 capsid trimer interface
item.description:
Yanan Zhu, Juan S. Rey, Juan Shen, Juan R. Perilla, Peijun Zhang
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78493-x
Abstract The HIV-1 capsid, composed of capsid (CA) proteins arranged into a conical surface lattice, serves as a critical platform for host–pathogen interactions. Many host cofactors regulate HIV-1 infection by selectively recognizing the higher-order CA lattice rather than individual monomers or capsomers. Among these, Myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB) is a key cellular restriction factor that binds the capsid via its N-terminal fragment containing an arginine-rich motif (RRR), blocking HIV-1 infection at early infection stages. However, the structural basis of this interaction has remained elusive. Here, we present a structural characterization of the CA lattice in complex with the MxB N-terminal fragment using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging. Combining cryoEM structures with EM-guided all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we identify residue-specific interactions between MxB and the CA trimer interfaces. Notably, residues 10-20 of the MxB N-terminus adopt an α-helical conformation that stabilizes binding at the CA trimer interface, revealing a distinct mode of capsid engagement. These findings provide insight into arginine-rich motif–mediated recognition by MxB and other host factors and establish a structural framework for the development of capsid-targeting antiviral therapeutics.

item.title: Survival and divergence of Arctic endemic cod species during 50,000 years of climate change
item.description:
Julek Chawarski, Flor Vermassen, Kim Vane, Hauke Flores, Jutta Wollenburg, Hendrik Grotheer, Claudia Morys, Nicole Hildebrandt, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78810-4
Abstract Despite significant climate variability in the Northern Hemisphere ~50,000–12,000 years ago, the potential for vertebrates to periodically thrive in the glacial Arctic Ocean has been largely overlooked because ecosystem productivity was assumed to be too low. Here, we analyze fish otoliths preserved in deep-sea sediments and find that two Arctic endemic cod species, ice cod ( Arctogadus glacialis ) and polar cod ( Boreogadus saida ), lived at 87–89 °N ~ 48,000–35,000 years ago and reappeared at the onset of the Holocene ~12,000 years ago. A. glacialis also occurred north of Greenland at 84–85 °N ~ 20,000 years ago, during the peak of the Last Glacial Maximum, suggesting the presence of refugia that enabled survival and divergence from B. saida under the harshest climate conditions. These findings suggest that the glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but rather a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish.

item.title: Explainable artificial intelligence reveals spatially divergent effects of global change on mammals
item.description:
Lei Song, Amy E. Frazier, Peter Kedron, Diogo S. A. Araujo, Diyang Cui, Brian J. Enquist, César Hinojo-Hinojo, Joana M. Krieger, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78677-5
Abstract Understanding how global change reshapes species distributions remains a central challenge in ecology, yet most global assessments treat environmental drivers as static, uniform, or aggregate influences. This obscures where, why, and how specific drivers generate ecological risk or opportunity. Here, we apply explainable machine learning to assess how climate averages, variability, extremes, and land cover are projected to reshape future distributions of 1,992 terrestrial mammals. Using Shapley Additive Explanations with species distribution models, we quantify the directional contribution of 16 environmental drivers and track how these contributions change over space and time. We propose two ecological diagnostics, directional turnovers and favorability shifts, that reveal where drivers switch from favorable to unfavorable, or the reverse, and where their influence strengthens or weakens without sign reversal. While not designed to infer causation, our framework assesses whether projected spatial patterns align with ecological expectations. We show that climate extremes impose intense but spatially restricted impacts, temperature-related drivers dominate exposure patterns, particularly for specialist species, and the same driver can impose risk in one region while creating opportunity in another. By decomposing projected biodiversity change into driver-specific signatures, our framework advances biodiversity forecasting toward a more actionable understanding of ecological risk and opportunity.

item.description:

DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78454-4
Abstract Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.
